_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
tosafot:a1.1: That this one that had not given birth is superior: so too in the first chapter of Temura (8b): Mar Zutra visited the house of Rav Ashi. They cut meat before him [and] said to him: Let the Master taste, for it is choice, since it is a firstborn. And “egla tilta” [the “third” calf] does not mean, as Rashi explained, the third of its mother’s womb, as we say in Sanhedrin (65b), “They would prepare for themselves an egla tilta”; rather, “tilta” is a term of importance, as in “and officers [shalishim] over all of them” (Exodus 14:7).
rashi:a2.1: Mishna. Born by caesarean section [yotzei dofen]: a firstborn that emerged through the side. The one that comes after it is a firstborn (for males and not) for the womb, and not for birth, since another one already emerged before it. [The words in parentheses are bracketed in the printed text.]
rashi:a2.2: Both of them must graze etc.: since they are uncertain firstborns, for Rabbi Tarfon is uncertain whether one that is a firstborn in one aspect is a firstborn or is not a firstborn.
gershom:a1.1: Born by caesarean section: that did not emerge through the womb itself, but, for example, they cut [the mother] open and it emerged from the side; or as we say in [the chapter] Behema HaMaksha, that the walls of the womb were cut away and then it emerged.
gershom:a2.1: And the one that comes after it: through the womb; for example, the womb healed again. It had been cut before, and afterward this one emerged from a whole womb.
gershom:a3.1: Both of them must graze etc.: because the one born by caesarean section is a firstborn for birth, and the one that comes after it is a firstborn for the womb. Rabbi Akiva says: Neither of them etc.
gershom:a4.1: A firstborn in one aspect: it is a firstborn either for birth or for the womb, even though it is not a firstborn in every respect. For in three things it must be a firstborn: for birth, for the womb and for males. To Rabbi Akiva it is obvious [that] a firstborn in one aspect [is not a firstborn]; that is, if it lacks one of these three, it is not a firstborn.
rashi:a4.1: Gemara. From a generalization that requires a detail: the generalization needs the detail to be with it.
rashi:a4.2: From a detail that requires a generalization: there is [a case] where the detail needs the generalization to be with it.
tosafot:a4.1: In brief: “How so? Sanctify to Me all the firstborn.” Rashi explained that this is a generalization and a detail: “firstborn” is the generalization, “male” the detail, and the generalization includes only what is in the detail. This first clause is not the explanation of “a generalization that requires a detail”; the middle and last clauses are: “If ‘male’, one might think even if a female emerged before it; the verse states: ‘that which opens the womb’,” and this one did not open the womb first. That is a generalization that requires a detail, since you cannot understand what the generalization says until the detail explains it, for “firstborn” can be read several ways: first of all the offspring; first for the womb though not first of the offspring (one that came through the womb after one born by caesarean section); or first of the males though a female preceded it through the womb. The detail explains that it is called a firstborn only if it is first for the womb, having opened the womb. Similarly in Kisui HaDam (Ḥullin 88b), on “and cover it with earth”: one might think he may cover it with a stone or overturn a vessel on it; the verse states “with earth.” [The Gemara there] asks: say “and cover it” is a generalization and “with earth” a detail, so the generalization includes only the detail; and answers that it is a generalization that requires a detail, which is not judged as a generalization and detail, since covering can be done two ways, with something coarse such as a stone or a vessel, or with something fine, so “with earth” was written to explain that the verse speaks of covering with something fine that mixes with [the blood]. [So far Rashi.] Tosafot: Rashi’s explanation fits Ravina below, who says a firstborn in one aspect is a firstborn. But the conclusion of our passage is that it is clear as Abaye, that a firstborn in one aspect is not a firstborn, and for Abaye it is not a generalization that requires a detail at all, since “firstborn” can be explained only one way. One could explain for Abaye that without the detail I would have said that even one born by caesarean section is a firstborn, since it is first of the offspring though not first for the womb. The Ri explains for Abaye: “firstborn” and “that which opens the womb” are each both a generalization and a detail, and each needs the other; each leaves one thing unspecified and specifies one: “firstborn” implies even one born by caesarean section, and “that which opens the womb” excludes it; “that which opens the womb” implies even one that came after one born by caesarean section, and “firstborn” excludes it. Rabbeinu Tam explains that both here and in Ḥullin it is a full generalization and detail: “firstborn” in general means either way and the detail comes to restrict it; “and cover it” means covering with a vessel or with earth, as one wishes, and the detail means earth specifically. What the Gemara there counts as a generalization that requires a detail does not refer to overturning the vessel in that baraita, but to another exposition at the beginning of that chapter (Ḥullin 83b), from the letter bet of “with earth” [ba’afar]: one must put earth below and earth above, for from “and cover it” we understand only above, not below; it is counted a generalization that requires a detail because of the extra bet in the detail, not because of the detail itself. And in our passage [the baraita] comes to explain a detail that requires a generalization, as the last clause teaches: “If ‘that which opens the womb’, one might think even one that emerged after one born by caesarean section; the verse states ‘firstborn’,” as Rashi explained. And although it teaches “from a generalization that requires a detail and from a detail that requires a generalization; how so?”, implying that it also comes to explain a generalization that requires a detail, it mentioned that only in passing; the main point is a detail that requires a generalization. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
rashi:a4.3: How so? Sanctify to Me etc.: this first clause is not an explanation of “a generalization that requires a detail”; rather the middle clause and the last clause are.
gershom:a5.1: All the firstborn: this is the generalization, which implies every firstborn, male or female. The verse states “male,” which is the detail, to exclude a female.
rashi:a4.4: “All the firstborn”: a generalization, even females. The verse states “male”: “every firstborn that is born in your herd and in your flock, the male” (Deuteronomy 15:19). This is the generalization and detail taught in the first of the thirteen principles [of exegesis], where the detail comes to restrict the generalization from its plain meaning and confine it to the detail, and the generalization includes only what is in the detail. For this resembles the generalization and detail taught with the first principle: “of the animals” is a generalization, “of the herd and of the flock” is a detail; the generalization includes only what is in the detail.
rashi:a5.1: If [it said only] “firstborn male”: one might think even if a female emerged before it through the womb, for this is what “firstborn male” implies: a firstborn among males; since no other male preceded it, it is a firstborn, even though it is not a firstborn for birth or for the womb.
rashi:a5.2: The verse states: “That which opens the womb”: this detail was needed to explain that it is not called a firstborn unless it is a firstborn for the womb, because we would not have known what the generalization meant. It is not like a generalization and a detail, where the detail serves to restrict the generalization and not to explain its meaning, such as the first clause of the baraita: “Firstborn: one might think even a female; the verse states: male.” That is a full generalization and detail, for [the detail] was not needed to explain what a firstborn is, since a female is a firstborn in every respect; rather it comes to restrict, lest you say that females too are sanctified as firstborn. Similarly in Sheḥitat Ḥullin (Ḥullin 88b), “and cover it with earth” is called a generalization that requires a detail, because there are two kinds of covering: such as overturning a vessel over it, and covering with something that scatters, such as earth and the like. Therefore “earth” is stated, to exclude covering with a whole object; and we do not judge it as a full generalization and detail, [for then] we would also exclude ground stones, plaster and arsenic.
gershom:a6.1: One might think even if a female emerged before it through the womb: for it is still a firstborn for males.
gershom:a7.1: The verse states: “That which opens the womb”: for we also require a firstborn for the womb.
rashi:a5.3: One might think even if it emerged after one born by caesarean section: and it itself emerged through the womb.
rashi:a5.4: “Firstborn”: which implies that we require a firstborn in every respect. This is a detail that requires a generalization: “male” and “that which opens the womb,” which are a detail, need “firstborn,” for had “firstborn” not been stated, I would have said that even though it is not a firstborn it is sanctified. Most details in the Torah do not need the generalizations that accompany them; for example, “of the herd and of the flock” (Leviticus 1:2) did not need “of the animals” to be written, and “If a man gives his neighbor a donkey [or an ox] or a sheep” (Exodus 22:9) does not need “or any animal”; rather [the generalization] comes to add to the detail. A generalization that requires a detail: you cannot understand what it says until the detail comes and explains it. For example, “firstborn male: one might think even if a female emerged before it”: for “firstborn,” which is the generalization, I do not know in what sense it is said: whether for males even though not for the womb, as in this case; or for the womb and not for males, such as a male that opened the womb after one born by caesarean section; or else only when it is a firstborn both for the womb and for the offspring.
gershom:a8.1: If [only] “that which opens the womb”: this is a detail and a generalization, for from it one would understand only [a firstborn] for the womb.
gershom:a9.1: One might think even if it emerged after a female born by caesarean section; the verse states “firstborn”: which is the detail [emended: the generalization], and we require a firstborn in every respect, and this one is not a firstborn for birth.
rashi:a6.1: In the first clause, the baraita does not cite “firstborn”: he calls the middle clause “the first clause,” which teaches: “One might think even if a female emerged before it; the verse states: that which opens the womb.” Since the baraita did not cite “the verse states: firstborn,” which would imply a firstborn in every respect, evidently it does not take [the word] to mean a firstborn in every respect; and that is why it did not cite it, since this case would not be excluded by it: since no male emerged before it, we call it a firstborn, for it is a firstborn for males. Evidently he holds that the “firstborn” of the verse means even a firstborn in one aspect.
tosafot:a6.1: In the first clause the baraita does not cite “firstborn”; evidently a firstborn in one aspect is a firstborn: this implies that since a firstborn in one aspect is a firstborn, we would obligate even where a female emerged before it, were it not for “that which opens the womb.” And this is puzzling: Rabbi Tarfon, who is uncertain, should have obligated [that case] out of uncertainty, like one born by caesarean section and the one that follows it, since he does not exclude one born by caesarean section by “that which opens the womb.” One may answer: although he does not consider it reasonable to exclude one born by caesarean section by “that which opens the womb,” since it is [included among the offspring], whether of males or of females, at the least [the phrase] comes to exclude the case where a female emerged before it; for otherwise, why do I need “that which opens the womb” that the Merciful One wrote?
gershom:a10.1: In the first clause it does not cite “firstborn” [meaning] in every respect: this is the first clause, “If ‘male’ etc., the verse states: that which opens the womb.” That is, since it does not say “the verse states: firstborn,” it implies that it holds that even though it emerged after a female born by caesarean section, it is a firstborn, since it is a firstborn for the womb and for males. Evidently a firstborn in one aspect is a firstborn.
gershom:a11.1: And even though it is a firstborn in two respects, since it lacks one, it is called a firstborn in one aspect.
rashi:a6.2: And in the last clause the baraita does cite “firstborn”: evidently the “firstborn” written in the verse means in every respect, so that a firstborn in one aspect, such as this one, which is a firstborn for the womb (and for males) but not a firstborn for the offspring, is not a firstborn. [The words in parentheses are bracketed in the printed text.]
gershom:a12.1: The last clause cites “firstborn”: this is the last clause, “If ‘that which opens the womb’”; evidently it requires a firstborn in every respect. And the first clause contradicts the last.
rashi:a7.1: Actually, a firstborn in one aspect is not a firstborn: that is, the verse means in every respect. And as for the baraita not citing “firstborn” in the first clause:
rashi:a7.2: This is what it is saying: If [only] “male,” one might think even if it emerged through the side; the verse states “that which opens the womb”: for here the baraita cannot cite “firstborn” to exclude it, since it is a firstborn in every respect, as no other preceded it in the world. That is why it took “that which opens the womb,” and as a matter of course the case where a female emerged before it is also excluded by “that which opens the womb.”
gershom:a13.1: Actually etc. And the first clause is to be explained thus: “If ‘male’, one might think even if it itself emerged through the side it is the firstborn; the verse states: that which opens the womb,” and this one did not open the womb. And now, since it does not teach “one might think even if a female emerged before it through the womb; the verse states: that which opens the womb,” from which we would infer that if a female emerged before it through the side it is a firstborn even so, but rather teaches “one might think even if it emerged through the side,” from which nothing can be inferred, since it does not speak of a female at all, [the printed text is corrupt here; an editor suggests: one may well say that we require a firstborn in every respect, as in the last clause] conclude from it that we require a firstborn in every respect, as in the last clause.
rashi:a8.1: Ravina says: a firstborn in one aspect is a firstborn: that is, the [word] “firstborn” of the verse means even in one aspect. And as for the last clause, where the baraita cites “firstborn” to exclude one that emerged after one born by caesarean section: this is not derived from the meaning of the verse, for the verse means a firstborn [even] in one aspect, but from the extra word of the verse.
gershom:a14.1: Ravina says: Actually, a firstborn in one aspect: one that lacks one thing only is a firstborn, as we inferred initially from the first clause.
rashi:a8.2: For if it enters your mind etc., “firstborn” that the Merciful One wrote: which implies that it is a firstborn in part; why do I need it? Let it write “that which opens the womb… the male, you shall sanctify,” and be silent.
gershom:a15.1: And the last clause, which seems to you to require a firstborn in every respect, explain thus; and this is what it is saying: If it enters your mind that a male that emerged after one born by caesarean section is sanctified, why do I need “firstborn” that the Merciful One wrote?
rashi:b1.1: For if to exclude where a female emerged before it: through the womb, that is derived from “that which opens the womb.” Rather, [it is] to exclude one that emerges after one that emerged by caesarean section. Between Abaye and Ravina there is no [practical difference]; they disagree only about the meaning of the verse. [The printed text reads “Rava,” corrected in brackets to “Ravina.”]
gershom:b1.1: If to exclude where a female emerged before it through the womb, that is derived from “that which opens the womb.”
gershom:b2.1: Rather, conclude from it: “firstborn” is to exclude one that emerged after one born by caesarean section, a male, which is not sanctified, since we require a firstborn for the womb and for males. But if a female emerged before it by caesarean section, even so it is a firstborn, even though it is not a firstborn for birth. Evidently a firstborn in one aspect, lacking only one thing, is a firstborn.
rashi:b2.1: If it enters your mind that a firstborn in one aspect: is the meaning of “firstborn,” and one that emerged after one born by caesarean section is excluded not by the meaning [of the word] but by its being extra: that works well where a male emerged first by caesarean section and then another male emerged through the womb; that one is excluded by the extra word of the verse, for it stands to reason that the verse comes to exclude it, since it is only a firstborn for the womb, while firstborn for males and for birth are lacking.
gershom:b3.1: Rav Aḥa of Difti said to Ravina: That works well. That is: granted, what you said, that where a male emerged by caesarean section and a male firstborn through the womb it is not sanctified, since you exclude it by “firstborn”: that works for me, since we require a firstborn in every respect.
rashi:b3.1: But where a female emerged by caesarean section: and then a male emerged through the womb, let it be sanctified, for it is a firstborn in two respects, for the womb and for males; and from the extra word of the verse you can exclude only one [case]. It stands to reason that it excludes one that emerged after a male born by caesarean section, and not one after a female born by caesarean section. So why does the baraita teach without qualification “even one that emerged after one born by caesarean section,” without distinguishing between male and female?
gershom:b4.1: But what you said, that where a female emerged by caesarean section and the male firstborn through the womb [it is not sanctified]: let it be sanctified, since it is a firstborn for males and a firstborn for the womb. [An editor’s note suggests reading: “…it is not sanctified: why? Let it be sanctified, since there is a firstborn for males and a firstborn for the womb. Rather, it is clear as Abaye.” The printed text then adds in parentheses: Why should it be sanctified? Didn’t the Merciful One write “every firstborn that is born”? Evidently it also requires a firstborn for birth.]
gershom:b6.1: (Rav Aḥa of Difti said to Ravina: That works well where a male emerged by caesarean section and a male through the womb, which is not sanctified, since it is excluded by “firstborn”: there is a firstborn for the womb, [but] no firstborn for males. But where a female emerged by caesarean section and a male through the womb, would you say so? Let it be sanctified, since there is a firstborn for males and a firstborn for the womb! Rather, it is clear as Abaye.) [This parenthesized comment is printed as a second version of the comments above.]
rashi:b3.2: Rather, it is clear as Abaye: that its meaning is a firstborn in every respect; therefore all of them are excluded.
gershom:b5.1: Rather, it is clear as Abaye: who explained: actually, a firstborn in one aspect is not a firstborn, and the first clause is saying thus [etc.]; and so we learn the principle.
rashi:b4.1: We will return to you, HaLoke’aḥ Ubar Parato.
rashi:b5.1: Mishna. One who purchases an animal: [the opening words of the new chapter].
rashi:b5.2: A goat in its first year: that gave birth within its year.
rashi:b5.3: Certainly: that offspring is for the priest, since before that it had not given birth.
rashi:b5.4: Uncertain: it grazes and is eaten in its blemish by the owner. For an uncertain firstborn donkey, he separates a lamb, and it is his own.
gershom:b8.1: A goat in its first year: he bought it, and it gave birth at the end of its year.
gershom:b9.1: Certainly for the priest: for it is a firstborn, since within its year it did not give birth before now.
gershom:b10.1: From then on: if he bought it older than a year, and it gave birth.
gershom:b11.1: Uncertain: whether it gave birth before or not; it is an uncertain firstborn, and it grazes and is eaten in its blemish.
gershom:b12.1: And likewise a ewe in its second year is certainly for the priest: for before that it does not give birth.
gershom:b13.1: And a cow or a donkey in their third year is certainly for the priest; from then on, uncertain. And for an uncertain donkey, in place of the grazing [that applies to] a kosher animal, he separates a lamb in place of this uncertain firstborn donkey, and it is his own.
tosafot:b5.1: Mishna. A cow or a donkey in their third year is certainly for the priest: one cannot explain that it [may] give birth within two years, but that had it given birth in the second year it would not give birth again in the third, even though a grown one gives birth every year, along the lines of what Rashi explained in the Gemara regarding a young goat, where it says that one that gave birth does not give birth again within its year, and Rashi explained: although grown ones give birth again within their year, young ones that gave birth do not give birth again within their year. One cannot explain so, for it is said explicitly at the beginning of Ein Ma’amidin (Avoda Zara 24b), regarding “and their calves they shut up at home” (I Samuel 6:10): “If [it was] less than three years old, does it give birth? But didn’t we learn: A cow or a donkey in their third year is certainly for the priest?” Conclude from it that within two years it does not give birth at all.
gershom:b14.1: If by offspring: by actual [offspring] alone were an animal exempted from the firstborn [obligation], it would be as you say: a goat in its first year is certainly for the priest etc.
rashi:b6.1: A murky discharge [tinuf]: explained in the Gemara. Perhaps it discharged within its year, which is a sign of offspring, and it was exempted from the firstborn [obligation]; therefore even a goat in its first year is uncertain.
rashi:b6.2: A fetal sac [shafir]: the skin of the form of the fetus.
tosafot:b6.1: And in a large animal an afterbirth, and in a woman a fetal sac and an afterbirth: in the chapter Behema HaMaksha (Ḥullin 77a) we learned: An afterbirth that partly emerged is forbidden for eating; as is the sign of offspring in a woman, so is the sign of offspring in an animal. This implies that it is more obvious in a woman than in an animal; and it is puzzling, for here we learned [that] an animal is like a woman. And some books do not read so there, but read: “a sign of offspring in a woman, a sign of offspring in an animal.” And my teacher says that the reading can be reconciled: since a fetal sac is not a sign of offspring in an animal as it is in a woman, it used this wording, [to say] that in any case an afterbirth is a sign of offspring in an animal as in a woman.
gershom:b15.1: But they said: the sign of offspring in a small animal is a murky discharge: if it miscarried blood from its womb, that blood was offspring, but it miscarried; that blood is called tinuf, and it stands in place of offspring, and [the animal] is exempted from the firstborn [obligation].
gershom:b16.1: And likewise a large animal: if the animal miscarried only an afterbirth, that is a sign of offspring, for there is no afterbirth without offspring, and it is exempted from the firstborn [obligation].
gershom:b17.1: And the sign of offspring in a woman is a fetal sac and an afterbirth. And the shafir is the blood inside the afterbirth. And one must be concerned that perhaps it discharged within its year and afterward gave birth at the end of five months; therefore everything is uncertain, even one in its first year.
gershom:b18.1: Any case where it is known that it had given birth: whether by a discharge or by birth, the priest has nothing here.
gershom:b19.1: And where it is known that it had not given birth: certainly, neither by a discharge nor by birth.
gershom:b20.1: And if uncertain: this is the purchaser, even [if the animal is] within its year.
gershom:b21.1: That discharged a hard clot of blood: for a clot too is a sign of offspring; and it is buried as the law of a firstborn, and [the animal] is thereafter exempt from the firstborn [obligation].
gershom:b22.1: And why uncertain: that is, that it is eaten only in its blemish.
gershom:b23.1: Let us say: follow etc., and it certainly gave birth within its year, and this one that it bore now, after its year, should be entirely non-sacred, and he may eat it without a blemish.
rashi:b8.1: Gemara. Rabbi Meir is concerned for the minority: as is taught below regarding a male minor and a female minor.
gershom:b24.1: Like Rabbi Meir: who is concerned for the minority, as is said below. There is also a minority of animals that do not give birth within their year; therefore it is uncertain.
gershom:b25.1: You may even say: Rabbi Yishmael holds like the Rabbis, who follow the majority.
rashi:b9.1: Nine stores: all of them sell meat of slaughtered animals and one sells meat of an unslaughtered carcass, and a piece of meat is found there on the ground: it is kosher, since whatever separates, separates from the majority. And this is a majority that is before us, since the stores are before us.
rashi:b9.2: And the Sanhedrin: for example, twelve acquit and eleven convict; he is acquitted.
tosafot:b9.1: With an evident majority, such as nine stores: he could have said, “And according to your reasoning, does Rabbi Meir disagree there? It is written: ‘Incline after the majority’ (Exodus 23:2),” and from there we derive [the case of] nine stores, in the first chapter of Ḥullin (11a).
gershom:b26.1: And when they follow the majority, it is with a majority that is before us, such as nine stores, all of them selling meat of slaughtered animals etc. Since there are nine stores before us, we say: whatever separates, separates from the majority. And the Sanhedrin, who follow the majority.
rashi:b9.3: A majority that is not before us: as here, where you said, follow the majority of animals in the whole world.
gershom:b27.1: But a majority that is not before us: (not born before us) [read: such as the majority of animals], they also follow the minority that do not give birth; therefore it is uncertain.
gershom:b28.1: A male minor and a female minor, which is a majority that is not before us: for we do not see the majority of the world, whether they are eunuchs or ailonit or not; and even so they follow the majority.
tosafot:b10.1: In brief: “Man” is written by the Merciful One, and we juxtapose woman to man: this implies here that a female minor’s ḥalitza is invalid by Torah law, like a male minor’s. This is puzzling: in the mishna in Mitzvat Ḥalitza (Yevamot 104b), the Jerusalem Talmud reads: “One who performs ḥalitza with a male minor, her ḥalitza is invalid; a female minor who performed ḥalitza performs ḥalitza again when she grows up, and if she did not, her ḥalitza is valid,” and so some of our books read; and the Gemara there says this is Rabbi Meir’s view, who says “man” is written in the section and we juxtapose woman to man. That implies Rabbi Meir concedes her ḥalitza is valid after the fact, and only ab initio she does not perform it, while for the Rabbis she performs it even ab initio; the Jerusalem Talmud too establishes it according to Rabbi Meir. Most of our books read “her ḥalitza is invalid,” but then it is difficult: [the mishna] should teach her together with the preceding clause, “a deaf man who received ḥalitza, a deaf woman who performed ḥalitza, one who performs ḥalitza with a male minor, and a female minor who performed ḥalitza: their ḥalitza is invalid”; and why does it say of a female minor “she performs ḥalitza again when she grows up” but not of a male minor; and it is obvious that if her ḥalitza is invalid she performs it again when she grows up. Therefore it seems that one reads “valid,” as in the Jerusalem Talmud, and one must say that the derivation here, juxtaposing woman to man, is a mere support, and the reason is a decree for a woman on account of a man, or alternatively a decree for ḥalitza on account of levirate marriage. So it seems from the Jerusalem Talmud on that mishna: Rabbi Shimon son of Rabbi Yosei asked before Rabbi: what is the difference between a male minor and a female minor? He said to him: “man” is written in the section, but here, “his yevama shall approach him before the elders,” in any case. Rabbi Mana stated it without attribution; Rabbi Yitzḥak son of Rabbi Ḥiyya Kahana in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan: it is Rabbi Meir, who says one does not perform ḥalitza or levirate marriage with a female minor lest she be found an ailonit; this implies it is all one reason. However, that does not seem right, for the Rabbis said to him, “You have aptly stated that one does not perform ḥalitza…,” and one does not perform levirate marriage with a female minor lest she be found an ailonit, and the Jerusalem Talmud mentions only the reason for levirate marriage; but the reason for not performing ḥalitza, if it is rabbinic, is a decree for a woman on account of a man. And according to the reading of our books, “invalid,” one may explain that it is not combined with the deaf man, deaf woman and male minor because those are according to everyone, while for a female minor there is a dispute; and it teaches “she performs ḥalitza again when she grows up” to teach that only according to the one who says it is invalid does she perform it again, but according to the one who says it is valid, she does not perform it again even ab initio. One can further say: according to the one who says at the beginning of Kol HaGet (Gittin 25a) that [the ḥalitza of] a minor and an anpalya are invalid and do not disqualify, it was needed to teach of a female minor “she performs ḥalitza” to teach that the ḥalitza is invalid but disqualifies [her for the brothers], and conclude from it that she does not enter levirate marriage. gershom:b29.1: For we learned etc.: “man” is written regarding ḥalitza and not regarding levirate marriage, as it is written: “And if the man does not wish” (Deuteronomy 25:7).
tosafot:b11.1: A male minor, lest he be found a eunuch: and if you say: according to the one who says in HaArel (Yevamot 80b) [that he is not a eunuch] until he has all [the signs], let us look whether, when he urinates, it forms an arch! One may answer: where he did not grow signs [of puberty] until most of his years, he is considered a eunuch even without the signs of a eunuch, as we say in HaArel (ibid.) and in Nidda (47b): “And if the signs of a eunuch did not appear, until when? Until most of his years.”
rashi:b11.1: Encounter a forbidden relative: since she is not fit to bear children, we do not apply to them “and it shall be that the firstborn whom she bears” (Deuteronomy 25:6), and the law of levirate marriage lapses for them, and they remain under the prohibition of a brother’s wife.
gershom:b30.1: And he is found to encounter a forbidden relative, and the mitzva of levirate marriage is not fulfilled.
gershom:b31.1: And the Rabbis: hold that one performs levirate marriage, for follow the majority of minors, even though it is not before us.
